strengths: Simple, low-cost idea (reversing step order via prompting, no added parameters) that is easy to integrate into existing PRM pipelines.

Very extensive empirical evaluation: 3 backbones (Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, Rho-Math-1B, Deepseek-Math-7B), 3 training objectives (BCE, MSE, Q-value ranking), 3 policy/sampling models, and 2 benchmarks (GSM-Plus, MATH500), yielding dozens of configurations with consistent improvements.
Ablation study (w/o L2R, w/o R2L) supports the claim that both directions contribute complementary signal rather than one direction dominating.
Qualitative case study illustrates a plausible mechanism by which backward verification can catch errors that forward-only scoring misses.
The method is framework-agnostic and could be adopted by other PRM training pipelines with minimal overhead.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification (Eqs. 2 and 6) is somewhat superficial: causal masking trivially yields zero partial derivatives w.r.t. future tokens by construction, and labeling this 'gradient vanishing' overstates the novelty of the diagnosis; the actual mechanism by which reversing step order helps a causal LM (which was never trained on such reversed, out-of-order text) is not carefully analyzed.

No baseline is included to disentangle whether gains stem from genuine bidirectional/backward verification versus simple two-stream ensembling/variance reduction (e.g., averaging two forward passes with different prompts/seeds). This is a critical missing control given the method essentially averages two scalar scores.

Training details for the R2L stream are underspecified: it is unclear whether the shared parameters fθ are trained on both forward and reversed trajectories jointly, or whether R2L scoring is applied zero-shot at inference to a model trained only in the forward direction; this ambiguity affects reproducibility and interpretation of results.

The claim of 'zero inference latency' is optimistic; while no new parameters are added, running two full forward passes through the same-sized backbone at minimum doubles compute/memory cost unless extra parallel hardware is available, and this trade-off is not discussed or measured.

No variance/error bars or repeated-seed results are reported despite many close-margin comparisons (differences of ~1-3 points in several configurations), making it hard to assess statistical significance of the reported gains.

The 'bidirectional' framing (analogy to BiLSTM) is somewhat of a stretch: the underlying model remains autoregressive/causal in each direction, so this is more accurately described as a dual-pass ensembling scheme over reversed step order rather than a jointly bidirectional architecture.

Comparisons to simpler alternative baselines (e.g., self-consistency, majority voting, or straightforward two-sample ensembling of standard L2R PRMs) are absent, limiting the ability to judge whether the specific 'reversed reasoning' mechanism is necessary for the observed gains.

strengths: Very extensive empirical validation: 3 LLM backbones (1B-7B scale), 3 training objectives, 3 sampling policies, 2 solution-level benchmarks and one step-level diagnostic benchmark, totaling 54 solution-level and 12 step-level configurations, with consistent improvements throughout.

Thorough and well-designed ablations, including removing each stream individually, comparing dynamic gating vs static averaging, and (importantly) comparing against homogeneous 2xL2R/2xR2L ensembles to rule out the possibility that gains are simply due to doubled compute rather than genuine bidirectional complementarity.

Practical efficiency: the method adds negligible parameters (0.3%) and, via parallel batched execution, only ~5% inference latency overhead, which is empirically verified with wall-clock measurements rather than only theoretical FLOPs.

Insightful analysis components beyond aggregate accuracy: step-wise MAE error distributions, visualization of learned gating weight evolution across reasoning progress, and both a positive and a negative (failure) case study that meaningfully discuss when retrospective (R2L) verification helps or fails.
Clear, well-organized writing and a simple, broadly applicable framework (architecture-agnostic, objective-agnostic) that could be adopted by future PRM work.
weaknesses: No direct empirical comparison against BiRM (Chen et al., 2025), which is explicitly identified in the introduction as the closest prior bidirectional PRM approach; the paper only argues qualitatively that BiRM is 'fundamentally forward-looking' without benchmarking against it, leaving the claimed advance over the most relevant baseline unverified.

The core mechanism (feeding a reversed step order into the same autoregressive base LLM to obtain an R2L reward) is under-justified: the paper does not clearly explain how/whether the R2L-PRM is separately fine-tuned on reversed sequences, nor discuss the training-cost implications (a full second PRM must presumably be trained for each backbone/objective combination), which is a hidden cost not reflected in the paper's efficiency claims that focus only on inference latency and gating parameters.

No variance/statistical significance reporting (e.g., across random seeds or multiple runs) despite the large number of configurations and some individually modest gains, making it hard to assess whether all reported differences are robust versus noise.

Novelty is somewhat incremental: architecturally, the method combines well-known ideas (BiLSTM-style bidirectional fusion, gating, sequence reversal) applied to PRMs; the primary innovation is the prompt-reversal implementation and the gating scheme, which is a relatively modest technical contribution.
Experimental scope is limited to mathematical reasoning tasks only (acknowledged as a limitation), so generalization to other domains such as code generation or open-ended reasoning is untested.

Case studies (Tables 5, 11, 12) are hand-picked qualitative illustrations rather than systematic quantitative error-type analysis, limiting how representative the discussed failure mode (arithmetic/algebraic skip errors) is of the model's overall weaknesses.
No code/artifact release is mentioned, which combined with underspecified R2L training details, may hinder full reproducibility despite detailed hyperparameter tables.
